SimpleHelp CVE-2026-48558 exposure: vulnerable/internet-facing servers (KEV) AIExploitation High
Surfaces hosts carrying the maximum-severity SimpleHelp OIDC auth-bypass CVE-2026-48558, prioritising internet-facing instances. This is the entry vector the actor exploited to forge a Technician session; CISA KEV mandates remediation by 2026-07-02. Rationale: Anchors on the exact CVE id (CVE-2026-48558) from the article and the KEV listing; the remediation target is SimpleHelp v5.5.16 per Horizon3.ai. Internet-facing pivot ranks the actual attack surface. Cross-checked against: • https://horizon3.ai/attack-research/vulnerabilities/cve-2026-48558/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/simplehelp-bug-lets-hackers-create-rogue-remote-support-accounts/
ATT&CKT1190 T1078.004
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Patched server still reporting stale TVM inventory until next scan
  • Internal-only SimpleHelp instance flagged internet-facing due to NAT/proxy misattribution
  • SimpleHelp deployment not using OIDC auth (not actually exploitable) still showing the CVE
  • Decommissioned host lingering in device inventory
Suppression filter
| where SoftwareVersion !startswith "5.5.16" and SoftwareVersion !startswith "6.0"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the host runs SimpleHelp server with OIDC/Azure AD OIDC auth enabled and version < 5.5.16; check IsInternetFacing/PublicIP. Step 2 (contain): Take the server off the public internet or apply v5.5.16+ immediately; audit Technician accounts and remove any unrecognised ones plus their self-enrolled MFA factors. Step 3 (hunt): Review SimpleHelp logs for new Technician logons with no preceding IdP sign-in and for script-execution/file-transfer actions; pivot managed endpoints to the node.exe/jquery.js and a.dev-tunnels.com detections.

TaskWeaver loader: node.exe executing jquery.js AIInstallation High
Detects the Node.js runtime executing a script named jquery.js — the obfuscated TaskWeaver loader dropped via the compromised SimpleHelp RMM channel. jquery.js is a browser-side library that is essentially never executed server-side through node. Rationale: node.exe + a script named jquery.js is the exact loader artifact named by Blackpoint and corroborated by BleepingComputer/SecurityWeek; cross-platform node binary covers the macOS/Linux variants the article calls out. Cross-checked against: • https://blackpointcyber.com/blog/a-djinn-in-the-machine-taskweavers-node-js-intrusion-chain/ • https://www.securityweek.com/critical-simplehelp-vulnerability-exploited-for-malware-delivery/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1106 T1072
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer running a build/test harness that happens to invoke a server file named jquery.js
  • Electron/Node desktop app bundling a jquery.js entry point
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sandbox
  • Internal automation that copies front-end assets and node-validates them
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\node_modules\", "\AppData\Roaming\npm") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.cmd","npm.exe","code.exe"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the full node.exe command line and parent process; confirm jquery.js path (often a temp/AppData dir) and whether the parent is the SimpleHelp agent/service. Hash and submit the jquery.js file. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, kill the node.exe process tree, and quarantine jquery.js. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep the estate for the same jquery.js name/hash and for node.exe beaconing to a.dev-tunnels.com; check the managing SimpleHelp server for rogue Technician activity.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "jquery.js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "node"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "jquery.js"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine

TaskWeaver C2 beacon to a.dev-tunnels.com from node.exe AICommand & Control Medium
Detects TaskWeaver's encrypted C2 to the dev-tunnels.com tunneling domain (a.dev-tunnels.com) initiated by the Node.js runtime. Pairs the documented C2 host with a node.exe initiator to separate malware traffic from legitimate developer use of Microsoft Dev Tunnels. Rationale: Uses the exact C2 host a.dev-tunnels.com from the article plus node.exe as initiator; constraining to the Node.js runtime is the noise-reducer that keeps legitimate Dev Tunnels usage out. Sentinel DNS telemetry lacks a process field, so it matches the host directly (noted as broader). Cross-checked against: • https://blackpointcyber.com/blog/a-djinn-in-the-machine-taskweavers-node-js-intrusion-chain/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-exploit-critical-simplehelp-flaw-deploy-new-djinn-infostealer-taskweaver-malware/
ATT&CKT1219 T1071.001 T1573.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer exposing a local Node.js service via Microsoft Dev Tunnels (VS Code port-forwarding)
  • CI runner using dev-tunnels for remote debugging
  • Legitimate node-based webhook tester resolving *.dev-tunnels.com
  • Sentinel DNS rule firing on any host (no process attribution) using Dev Tunnels
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "jquery.js" or RemoteUrl =~ "a.dev-tunnels.com"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the resolving/connecting process is node.exe and correlate to a jquery.js execution on the same host; check whether the user is a known developer authorised to use Dev Tunnels. Step 2 (contain): Block a.dev-tunnels.com (and unknown *.dev-tunnels.com) at egress, isolate the host, kill node.exe. Step 3 (hunt): Look for subsequent large outbound to 96.126.130.126:58942 and credential-store access by the same node process.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where RemoteUrl endswith "dev-tunnels.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery =~ "a.dev-tunnels.com" or DnsQuery endswith ".dev-tunnels.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, EventProduct

Djinn Stealer credential-store fan-out by node.exe AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects a single Node.js process touching multiple distinct developer/cloud credential stores (~/.aws, ~/.ssh, .npmrc, ~/.docker, AI-assistant configs, crypto wallets) in one pass — the signature collection behaviour of Djinn Stealer dropped by TaskWeaver. Rationale: Builds the cred-store list directly from the article's enumeration (AWS/Azure/GCP, SSH, npm/.docker, Claude/Gemini/Codex AI-assistant configs, Exodus/Electrum wallets); the high-fidelity signal is one node.exe hitting >=3 distinct stores in a single pass, which Djinn does by design. Cross-checked against: • https://blackpointcyber.com/blog/a-djinn-in-the-machine-taskweavers-node-js-intrusion-chain/ • https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks-data-breaches/djinn-stealer-targets-cloud-ai-credentials
ATT&CKT1555 T1552.001 T1552.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Node-based IaC/deploy tool (e.g. Pulumi, CDK, serverless) reading .aws + .kube + .docker during a deploy
  • Dev workstation backup/sync agent built on node copying dotfiles
  • A package manager (npm/pnpm) reading .npmrc plus auth configs during install
  • Security tooling enumerating cred stores for posture checks
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "jquery.js" or DistinctCredStores >= 5
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the node.exe command line and parent — TaskWeaver/jquery.js lineage vs a known dev tool; list which stores were touched and whether an archive was then written. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host and treat every touched credential as compromised — begin rotation of AWS/Azure/GCP keys, SSH keys, GitHub/npm tokens, and any AI-assistant API keys; revoke sessions. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on those credentials in cloud audit logs (CloudTrail/AzureActivity/gcp.audit) for anomalous use from new IPs, and search for tar.gz staging + egress to 96.126.130.126.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| extend P = tolower(strcat(FolderPath, "\\", FileName))
| where P has_any (".aws",".ssh",".npmrc",".docker",".claude","anthropic","gcloud",".kube","electrum","exodus","pulumi","vault-token",".config/gh","id_rsa")
| summarize DistinctCredStores = dcount(P), Stores = make_set(FolderPath, 25), FileCount = count(), TimeStart = min(Timestamp), TimeEnd = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| where DistinctCredStores >= 3
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "node"
| extend P = tolower(TargetFilePath)
| where P has_any (".aws",".ssh",".npmrc",".docker",".claude","anthropic","gcloud",".kube","electrum","exodus","pulumi","vault-token","id_rsa")
| summarize DistinctCredStores = dcount(P), Stores = make_set(TargetFilePath, 25), TimeStart = min(TimeGenerated), TimeEnd = max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessId, ActingProcessCommandLine
| where DistinctCredStores >= 3
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\Node.exe) @TargetFilename:(*.aws* OR *.ssh* OR *npmrc* OR *.docker* OR *.claude* OR *anthropic* OR *gcloud* OR *electrum* OR *exodus* OR *vault*)
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo ContextImageFileName=/node(\.exe)?$/i
| TargetFileName=/(\.aws|\.ssh|\.npmrc|\.docker|\.claude|anthropic|gcloud|\.kube|electrum|exodus|pulumi|vault-token|id_rsa)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextProcessId], function=count(field=TargetFileName, distinct=true, as=DistinctStores))
| DistinctStores >= 3

Djinn Stealer exfiltration to 96.126.130.126:58942 AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects outbound connections to the actor's exfiltration server 96.126.130.126 on the documented non-standard high port TCP/58942, where Djinn ships the AES-256-GCM/RSA-2048-wrapped tar.gz of stolen credentials. Rationale: Hard IOC: the exact exfil endpoint 96.126.130.126:58942 named by Blackpoint. Matching the IP alone is high-fidelity (dedicated attacker infrastructure); port and initiating process are surfaced for triage. Cross-checked against: • https://blackpointcyber.com/blog/a-djinn-in-the-machine-taskweavers-node-js-intrusion-chain/ • https://www.securityweek.com/critical-simplehelp-vulnerability-exploited-for-malware-delivery/
ATT&CKT1041 T1048
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/sandbox detonation host deliberately contacting the IOC
  • Internal scanner or honeypot probing the IP
  • Stale NAT log re-attributing the connection to the wrong internal host
  • Analyst manually curl-ing the IP during investigation
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the initiating process (expect node.exe) and the bytes transferred; confirm whether a tar.gz/encrypted archive was staged just before. Step 2 (contain): Block 96.126.130.126 at perimeter and host firewall, isolate the source host, and capture memory/the archive for forensics. Step 3 (hunt): Treat all credentials on that host as exfiltrated and rotate; search every host for any contact with 96.126.130.126 or a.dev-tunnels.com and for the jquery.js loader.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "96.126.130.126"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "96.126.130.126"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkBytes, NetworkApplicationProtocol

Djinn Stealer Linux secret harvest via bulk /proc environ/cmdline reads AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects a Node.js process bulk-reading /proc/<pid>/environ and /proc/<pid>/cmdline across many PIDs on Linux — Djinn's technique to scrape passwords, API keys and DB strings passed via env vars and process arguments of other running processes. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's Linux-specific behaviour — reading /proc/<pid>/cmdline and /proc/<pid>/environ to surface secrets in args/env. node initiator plus fan-out across >=10 distinct PIDs distinguishes mass scraping from a process inspecting itself. Cross-checked against: • https://blackpointcyber.com/blog/a-djinn-in-the-machine-taskweavers-node-js-intrusion-chain/
ATT&CKT1057 T1552.001 T1082
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A node-based APM/observability agent reading /proc for process metrics
  • A container/orchestration sidecar enumerating /proc/<pid>/environ for health checks
  • A legitimate debugging tool inspecting environment of child processes
  • A monitoring exporter (e.g. node-exporter-style) scraping /proc
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node_exporter","datadog","newrelic","elastic-agent","pm2"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the node process lineage (TaskWeaver/jquery.js vs a known monitoring agent) and how many distinct PIDs' environ/cmdline were read. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, terminate the node process, and rotate any secrets known to be passed via environment variables/args on that host (DB strings, API tokens). Step 3 (hunt): Correlate with cred-store fan-out and tar.gz staging on the same host, and check egress to 96.126.130.126:58942 / a.dev-tunnels.com.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe")
| where FolderPath startswith "/proc/"
| where FileName in~ ("environ","cmdline")
| summarize ProcReads = dcount(FolderPath), Sample = make_set(FolderPath, 15), TimeStart = min(Timestamp), TimeEnd = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| where ProcReads >= 10
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "node"
| where TargetFilePath startswith "/proc/"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("environ","cmdline")
| summarize ProcReads = dcount(TargetFilePath), Sample = make_set(TargetFilePath, 15), TimeStart = min(TimeGenerated), TimeEnd = max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessId, ActingProcessCommandLine
| where ProcReads >= 10

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48558", "CVE-2026-20245")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48558", "CVE-2026-20245")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ToddyCat: your hidden email assistant. Part 2
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] ToddyCat Umbrij scheduled task masquerading as Kaspersky EDR (KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp) · [LLM] ToddyCat Umbrij DLL sideload — signed host EXE loading attacker DLL from writable path · [LLM] ToddyCat Umbrij command-line parameters (-deepsearch/-regex/-debugport/-browser/-domainAd) · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] ToddyCat STRD — Chromium browser launched with --remote-debugging-port by non-browser parent · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
ToddyCat Umbrij scheduled task masquerading as Kaspersky EDR (KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp) AIInstallation High
Hunts a scheduled task named 'KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp' used by ToddyCat to launch the digitally-signed sideload host for Umbrij. Kaspersky confirms it never creates a task with that name, so any task bearing it is the attacker masquerading malicious execution as a legitimate security agent. Rationale: Anchored on the literal task name 'KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp', which the vendor states it never legitimately creates — a near-zero-FP string unique to this campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-steals-email-data-from-outlook/118044/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/11/toddycats-new-hacking-tools-steal.html
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1036.004
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal red-team or purple-team exercise deliberately replaying ToddyCat TTPs
  • A SOC analyst manually recreating the task name during IOC validation/testing
  • Custom in-house monitoring task that copied the name as a decoy honeytoken
  • Backup/imaging tooling restoring a previously-compromised host snapshot that still contains the task
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("redteam-deploy.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the task's Actions/Command and the binary it launches; confirm path (expect c:\Users\Public\ or c:\windows\vss\) and Authenticode signer — a Bitdefender/Microsoft/Google-signed EXE running from a writable path is the tell. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, disable/delete the task, and revoke active Google/Gmail OAuth sessions for any user logged on (the tool steals live browser sessions). Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the launched binary for DLL sideloading (log.dll, GoogleServices.dll, Microsoft.VisualStudio.QualityTools.VideoRecorderEngine.dll) and for any child browser launched with --remote-debugging-port.
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "ScheduledTaskCreated"
| where AdditionalFields has "KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp"

ToddyCat Umbrij DLL sideload — signed host EXE loading attacker DLL from writable path AIInstallation High
Hunts the three legitimate, signed binaries ToddyCat abuses for DLL sideloading (BDSubWiz.exe→log.dll, VSTestVideoRecorder.exe→Microsoft.VisualStudio.QualityTools.VideoRecorderEngine.dll, GoogleDesktop.exe→GoogleServices.dll) when the sideloaded DLL is loaded from an anomalous writable directory such as C:\Users\Public\ or C:\Windows\vss\. The writable-path constraint discriminates the malicious load from legitimate installs. Rationale: Pairs the exact (host EXE, hijack DLL) tuples named in the article with the writable-path constraint (Users\Public, Windows\vss seen in the observed command lines) — the path is what separates the malicious side-load from legitimate Bitdefender/VS/Google installs. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-steals-email-data-from-outlook/118044/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/11/toddycats-new-hacking-tools-steal.html
ATT&CKT1574.002
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Bitdefender ConnectAgent / Visual Studio Test / Google Desktop installed to a non-standard custom path (rare; mitigated by writable-path filter)
  • Software-packaging or app-virtualization tools (e.g. App-V, MSIX) staging these binaries under Public
  • Forensic/IR sandbox detonating the sample for analysis
  • Backup/restore tooling rehydrating these files under C:\Windows\vss during a VSS operation
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the loading EXE's Authenticode signer is genuine (Bitdefender/Microsoft/Google) but running from C:\Users\Public or C:\Windows\vss — a real signed binary in a writable dir loading an unsigned same-named DLL is the side-load. Hash the DLL and check against the article's MD5 IOCs. Step 2 (contain): Isolate host, kill the host process tree, quarantine the DLL, and revoke OAuth/Gmail sessions for logged-on users. Step 3 (hunt): Search the scheduled-task masquerade (KasperskyEndpointSecurityEDRAvp) and any browser launched with --remote-debugging-port by this binary; sweep other hosts for the same hash/path.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "BDSubWiz.exe" and FileName =~ "log.dll")
     or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "VSTestVideoRecorder.exe" and FileName =~ "Microsoft.VisualStudio.QualityTools.VideoRecorderEngine.dll")
     or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "GoogleDesktop.exe" and FileName =~ "GoogleServices.dll")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Users\Public\", @"\Windows\vss\") or FolderPath has_any (@"\Users\Public\", @"\Windows\vss\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 7
| where (EventData has "BDSubWiz.exe" and EventData has "log.dll")
     or (EventData has "VSTestVideoRecorder.exe" and EventData has "Microsoft.VisualStudio.QualityTools.VideoRecorderEngine.dll")
     or (EventData has "GoogleDesktop.exe" and EventData has "GoogleServices.dll")
| where EventData has @"\Users\Public\" or EventData has @"\Windows\vss\"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, EventData
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: ToddyCat Umbrij DLL Side-Load from Writable Path
id: 2b8e4f17-3c6a-4e29-9d10-5a7b6c8d0e1f

ToddyCat STRD — Chromium browser launched with --remote-debugging-port by non-browser parent AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the core 'Shadow Token via Remote Debug' (STRD) technique: Umbrij launches Chrome/Edge in headless mode with a remote debugging port and drives the live Gmail session to mint an OAuth authorization code. The discriminator is a browser process bearing --remote-debugging-port whose parent is NOT explorer or the browser itself (e.g. the Umbrij sideload host). Rationale: The --remote-debugging-port flag is essentially never used in normal enterprise browsing (corroborated by Elastic/SpecterOps cookie-theft research); requiring a non-browser parent (the Umbrij sideload host) makes it specific to the STRD OAuth-theft chain rather than a developer launching a debug instance. Cross-checked against: • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/security/7.17/prebuilt-rule-0-16-2-potential-cookies-theft-via-browser-debugging.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/11/toddycats-new-hacking-tools-steal.html
ATT&CKT1185 T1528 T1539
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Front-end/QA developers running Selenium/Puppeteer/Playwright automation that launches Chrome with --remote-debugging-port
  • Electron or CEF-based apps spawning a Chromium child with a debug port
  • Browser performance/profiling tooling launched by an IDE
  • Automated UI test runners on build/CI agents
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("node.exe","python.exe","chromedriver.exe","msedgedriver.exe","electron.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the parent process — a developer automation tool (node.exe, python.exe, chromedriver.exe) is likely benign; a signed-but-misplaced binary (BDSubWiz/GoogleDesktop/VSTestVideoRecorder) or unknown parent is malicious. Check whether the same host shows the Kaspersky-named scheduled task or a side-loaded DLL. Step 2 (contain): Isolate host, kill the browser+parent tree, and immediately revoke the user's Google/Gmail OAuth tokens and active sessions (the code may already be exchanged for an access token). Step 3 (hunt): Review Google Workspace/Gmail API access logs for token grants and unusual app/API reads near the event time; sweep for the same parent binary org-wide.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("BDSubWiz.exe","VSTestVideoRecorder.exe","GoogleDesktop.exe","bds.exe")
     or InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","userinit.exe","svchost.exe")
| extend Headless = ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--headless","--remote-debugging-pipe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, Headless
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\chrome.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\msedge.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\brave.exe"
| where CommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where not(ParentProcessName endswith "\\explorer.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\chrome.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\msedge.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\userinit.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Chromium Browser Remote Debugging Port Launched by Non-Browser Parent (ToddyCat STRD)
id: 9c1d7a3e-5f48-4b62-8e09-2a6b3c4d5e6f
description: Detects the ToddyCat Umbrij STRD technique - Chrome/Edge launched with --remote-debugging-port by a parent process that is not explorer or the browser, used to drive a live Gmail session and steal an OAuth authorization code.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-umbrij-tool-and-oauth/120251/
  - https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/security/7.17/prebuilt-rule-0-16-2-potential-cookies-theft-via-browser-debugging.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/30
tags:

  - attack.t1528

logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\chrome.exe'
      - '\msedge.exe'
      - '\brave.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: '--remote-debugging-port'
  filter_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\explorer.exe'
      - '\chrome.exe'
      - '\msedge.exe'
      - '\userinit.exe'
  condition: selection and not filter_parent
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\chrome.exe OR *\Chrome.exe OR *\msedge.exe OR *\MsEdge.exe OR *\brave.exe) @CommandLine:*remote-debugging-port* -@ParentImage:(*\explorer.exe OR *\Explorer.exe OR *\chrome.exe OR *\msedge.exe OR *\userinit.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\(chrome|msedge|brave)\.exe$/i CommandLine=/--remote-debugging-port/i
| NOT ParentBaseFileName=/^(explorer|chrome|msedge|brave|userinit)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe")) Processes.process="*--remote-debugging-port*" NOT (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","userinit.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe")) Processes.process="*--remote-debugging-port*" NOT (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","userinit.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| sort - lastTime
ToddyCat Umbrij command-line parameters (-deepsearch/-regex/-debugport/-browser/-domainAd) AIInstallation High
Hunts the distinctive Umbrij command-line switches regardless of which signed host binary carries them, catching renamed loaders. Targets the article's observed combinations: -regex with -deepsearch (profile/email selection), -debugport with -browser (debug-port + target browser), plus -runas-currentuser, -domainAd and -savepdf. Rationale: The switch combinations (-deepsearch + -regex; -debugport + -browser; plus the unique -domainAd/-savepdf/-runas-currentuser flags) are documented Umbrij parameters and are highly improbable in benign tooling, so they catch the tool even when the signed loader is renamed. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/toddycat-apt-steals-email-data-from-outlook/118044/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/11/toddycats-new-hacking-tools-steal.html
ATT&CKT1528 T1134.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Bespoke internal admin script that happens to use a -regex plus -deepsearch flag combination
  • Backup/PDF-export utility using a -savepdf switch
  • Domain-join automation tooling using a -domainAd-style argument
  • Red-team replay of the Umbrij command lines during validation
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Capture the full command line and the executing binary's signer/path; correlate with the scheduled-task masquerade and any side-loaded DLL on the host. Note any -debugport/-browser values to know which browser/port was targeted. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, terminate the process, and revoke Gmail/Google OAuth sessions and tokens for affected users. Step 3 (hunt): Look for the spawned headless browser with --remote-debugging-port, explorer.exe token duplication (T1134.003), and Google Workspace API access from the stolen token; sweep other hosts for the same flag patterns.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "-deepsearch" and ProcessCommandLine has "-regex")
     or (ProcessCommandLine has "-debugport" and ProcessCommandLine has "-browser")
     or (ProcessCommandLine has "-browser" and ProcessCommandLine has "-path" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("both","msedge","chrome"))
     or ProcessCommandLine has "-runas-currentuser"
     or ProcessCommandLine has "-domainAd"
     or ProcessCommandLine has "-savepdf"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (CommandLine has "-deepsearch" and CommandLine has "-regex")
     or (CommandLine has "-debugport" and CommandLine has "-browser")
     or (CommandLine has "-browser" and CommandLine has "-path" and (CommandLine has "msedge" or CommandLine has "chrome" or CommandLine has "both"))
     or CommandLine has "-runas-currentuser"
     or CommandLine has "-domainAd"
     or CommandLine has "-savepdf"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard Installation High
ConnectWise / AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installed outside IT change windows = common tradecraft for ransomware affiliates and IT-helpdesk impersonators.
ATT&CKT1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe")
   or FileName matches regex @"(?i)kaseya.*\.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer_Service.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\atera_agent.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\SplashtopStreamer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\RustDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\NinjaOne.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66") or SHA1 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66") or MD5 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66") or SHA1 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66") or MD5 in~ ("1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["1AB58838E5790EFB22F2D35AB98C0B7D", "A7D7D6C4C3F227F7117261C63B9E23A9", "3D3A621F852C42D97FD7260681E42508", "3432DD9AC0DF80EF86EB80BD080F839B", "22AAEB4946BA6D2F2E27FEB7DBB295DE", "F61FBFB7AA1CD5DC8F70B055B51563E2", "F169D6D172DFB775895A5E2B1540C854", "9F5F2F0FB0A7F5AA9F16B9A7B6DAD89F", "28CB7B261F4EB97E8A4B3B0D32F8DEF1", "BAE82A15D1DBFB024617B9B56A8E5F66"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Blackfield (BlackFL) ransomware encryption: .BlackFL extension + BlackField_ReadMe.txt note drop · [LLM] Blackfield ransomware Volume Shadow Copy deletion via WMIC (inhibit recovery) · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Blackfield (BlackFL) ransomware encryption: .BlackFL extension + BlackField_ReadMe.txt note drop AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the file-system signature of Blackfield/BlackFL ransomware encryption: files renamed/created with the unique '.BlackFL' extension and the dropping of the 'BlackField_ReadMe.txt' (or Feb-2026 variant 'BlackField-ReadMe.txt') ransom note. Both strings are unique to this family — corroborated across PCrisk, EnigmaSoft and WatchGuard — so this is article/campaign-specific rather than a generic mass-rename heuristic. Rationale: Anchored on two strings unique to this family and confirmed by second sources (PCrisk, WatchGuard): the '.BlackFL' encrypted-file extension and the 'BlackField_ReadMe.txt'/'BlackField-ReadMe.txt' ransom note. Neither appears in benign software, giving very high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.pcrisk.com/removal-guides/33312-blackfl-ransomware • https://www.watchguard.com/wgrd-security-hub/ransomware-tracker/blackfield • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/blackfield-ransomware-asks-nidec-corporation-for-2-million-ransom/
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware-analysis sandbox or researcher host holding sample files that already carry the '.BlackFL' extension
  • A security awareness/IR test or purple-team exercise intentionally dropping a file named BlackField_ReadMe.txt
  • Backup or quarantine archive that preserved previously-encrypted '.BlackFL' files being restored to a host
  • A threat-intel document or zip containing the ransom note text saved with the literal note filename
Suppression filter
| where AffectedFolders >= 2 or RansomNoteDropped >= 1   // single isolated .BlackFL sample with no note is likely a researcher/backup artifact
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: On the alerting DeviceName, pull the InitiatingProcess/SHA256 that wrote the files and check whether '.BlackFL' files span multiple folders (mass-rename = live encryption vs. a single benign sample). Confirm the BlackField_ReadMe.txt note timestamp. 2) CONTAIN: Immediately network-isolate the host via EDR, suspend/kill the initiating process, and disable the involved account; preserve a memory image before reimaging. 3) HUNT: Pivot the initiating-process SHA256 and the writing account across all hosts; search for the WMIC shadow-copy deletion (UC2), recent SMB share enumeration, and lateral logons from the same account to scope blast radius across the Nidec Chaun Choung subnet.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where FileName endswith ".BlackFL"
    or FileName matches regex @"(?i)BlackField[_-]ReadMe\.txt"
| summarize EncryptedFileCount = countif(FileName endswith ".BlackFL"),
            RansomNoteDropped = countif(FileName matches regex @"(?i)BlackField[_-]ReadMe\.txt"),
            AffectedFolders = dcount(FolderPath),
            SampleFiles = make_set(FileName, 8),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            InitiatingProcess = any(InitiatingProcessFileName),
            InitiatingProcessSHA256 = any(InitiatingProcessSHA256),
            InitiatingCmd = any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
        by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessId
| where EncryptedFileCount >= 1 or RansomNoteDropped >= 1
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".BlackFL"
    or TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)BlackField[_-]ReadMe\.txt"
| summarize EncryptedFileCount = countif(TargetFileName endswith ".BlackFL"),
            RansomNoteDropped = countif(TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)BlackField[_-]ReadMe\.txt"),
            AffectedPaths = dcount(TargetFilePath),
            SampleFiles = make_set(TargetFileName, 8),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            Process = any(ActingProcessName)
        by DvcHostname, ActingProcessId
| where EncryptedFileCount >= 1 or RansomNoteDropped >= 1
| order by FirstSeen desc
title: Blackfield (BlackFL) Ransomware Encryption Artifacts
id: 7c2f1e84-3b6a-4d2e-9f10-2a1b9c8d4e51
description: Detects file-system artifacts of Blackfield/BlackFL ransomware - files renamed/created with the .BlackFL extension or the BlackField_ReadMe.txt ransom note being dropped.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/blackfield-ransomware-asks-nidec-corporation-for-2-million-ransom/
  - https://www.pcrisk.com/removal-guides/33312-blackfl-ransomware
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/30
tags:
  - attack.impact
  - attack.t1486
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_ext:
    TargetFilename|endswith: '.BlackFL'
  selection_note:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - 'BlackField_ReadMe.txt'
      - 'BlackField-ReadMe.txt'
  condition: selection_ext or selection_note
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:(*.BlackFL OR *.blackfl OR *.BLACKFL) OR @TargetFilename:(*\\BlackField_ReadMe.txt OR *\\BlackField-ReadMe.txt OR *\\blackfield_readme.txt))
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/(\.BlackFL$|BlackField[_-]ReadMe\.txt$)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
| count >= 1
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_name) as file_name values(Filesystem.file_path) as file_path dc(Filesystem.file_path) as folder_count from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="*.BlackFL" OR Filesystem.file_name="BlackField_ReadMe.txt" OR Filesystem.file_name="BlackField-ReadMe.txt") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_id Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where count>=1 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - firstTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_name) as file_name values(Filesystem.file_path) as file_path dc(Filesystem.file_path) as folder_count from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="*.BlackFL" OR Filesystem.file_name="BlackField_ReadMe.txt" OR Filesystem.file_name="BlackField-ReadMe.txt") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_id Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where count>=1 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - firstTime
Blackfield ransomware Volume Shadow Copy deletion via WMIC (inhibit recovery) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the pre-encryption recovery-inhibition step documented for Blackfield/BlackFL: use of WMIC.exe to delete Volume Shadow Copies (with vssadmin as a fallback variant). Pairs with the encryption UC to give execution + impact coverage of the same intrusion before files are locked. Rationale: BlackField is documented (PCrisk/SOCRadar) to terminate recovery options by using WMIC.exe to delete Volume Shadow Copies; the wmic shadowcopy-delete and vssadmin delete-shadows command shapes are the concrete invocations. Medium fidelity because legitimate backup tooling can issue similar commands, hence the FP filter. Cross-checked against: • https://www.pcrisk.com/removal-guides/33312-blackfl-ransomware • https://www.ransomware.live/group/Blackfield • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/blackfield-ransomware-asks-nidec-corporation-for-2-million-ransom/
ATT&CKT1490 T1047
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Veeam / Acronis / Commvault backup jobs running pre-snapshot shadow-copy cleanup
  • Sysadmin manually troubleshooting VSS (vssadmin list/delete shadows) during storage maintenance
  • Windows imaging or DISM operations recycling shadow storage
  • SQL Server / Exchange backup maintenance scripts invoking WMIC shadowcopy operations
  • Endpoint management/SCCM task that prunes shadow copies on a schedule
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe","veeam.backup.manager.exe","acronis.exe","clussvc.exe","vsnapvss.exe","ccmexec.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the parent process (InitiatingProcessFileName) — a backup product (veeam, acronis) or services.exe-spawned admin tool is likely benign; an unsigned/unusual parent or one running from a temp path is high-risk. Check the same host for '.BlackFL' files (UC1). 2) CONTAIN: If the parent is not an approved backup agent, isolate the host immediately and disable the executing account before encryption completes. 3) HUNT: Sweep all hosts for the same parent SHA256, recent backup-deletion or bcdedit recovery-tampering commands, and the BlackField ransom note; review the account's logon history for lateral movement into the affected subsidiary network.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "shadowcopy" and ProcessCommandLine has "delete")
    or (FileName =~ "vssadmin.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_all ("delete","shadows"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "shadowcopy" and CommandLine has "delete")
    or (NewProcessName endswith "\\vssadmin.exe" and CommandLine has_all ("delete","shadows"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Blackfield Ransomware Volume Shadow Copy Deletion via WMIC
id: 2d9a7f3c-1e4b-4a8d-bc60-5f3e2d1a9b74
description: Detects WMIC.exe (with vssadmin fallback) deleting Volume Shadow Copies, the documented recovery-inhibition step of Blackfield/BlackFL ransomware prior to encryption.
references:
  - https://www.pcrisk.com/removal-guides/33312-blackfl-ransomware
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/blackfield-ransomware-asks-nidec-corporation-for-2-million-ransom/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/30
tags:
  - attack.impact
  - attack.t1490
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1047
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_wmic:
    Image|endswith: '\wmic.exe'
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'shadowcopy'
      - 'delete'
  selection_vss:
    Image|endswith: '\vssadmin.exe'
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'delete'
      - 'shadows'
  condition: selection_wmic or selection_vss
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 ((@Image:(*\\wmic.exe OR *\\WMIC.exe OR *\\WMIC.EXE) AND @CommandLine:(*shadowcopy* AND *delete*)) OR (@Image:(*\\vssadmin.exe OR *\\VSSADMIN.EXE) AND @CommandLine:(*delete* AND *shadows*)))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\(wmic|vssadmin)\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/shadow/i
| CommandLine=/delete/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as process values(Processes.parent_process) as parent_process from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where ((Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*shadowcopy*" AND Processes.process="*delete*") OR (Processes.process_name="vssadmin.exe" AND Processes.process="*delete*" AND Processes.process="*shadows*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | search user!="*$" | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - firstTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as process values(Processes.parent_process) as parent_process from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where ((Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*shadowcopy*" AND Processes.process="*delete*") OR (Processes.process_name="vssadmin.exe" AND Processes.process="*delete*" AND Processes.process="*shadows*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | search user!="*$" | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - firstTime
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |

    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:

            - '\MsMpEng.exe'

            - '\svchost.exe'

            - '\services.exe'

level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High

Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High

AirDrop and Quick Share Flaws Let Nearby Attackers Trigger Crashes and Bypass Checks

The Hacker News
2026-06-30 6 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Two researchers have found six security flaws in AirDrop and Quick Share, the wireless features that beam files between nearby devices with no cables or shared network. An attacker within wireless range, with just a laptop and no prior connection, can crash the sharing service on a Mac or iPhone set to receive from anyone, with no tap or prompt. The same research found Quick Share flaws that

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Repeated crashes of Google Quick Share for Windows (nearby_share.exe) — V6 use-after-free probing · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Repeated crashes of Google Quick Share for Windows (nearby_share.exe) — V6 use-after-free probing AIExploitation Medium
Hunts for repeated abnormal terminations of Google's Quick Share for Windows client (nearby_share.exe), the observable signature of a wireless/local-network attacker triggering the CISPA-disclosed heap use-after-free (V6) by colliding two connections. A single crash is benign; bursts of crashes on a network-facing sharing service indicate a nearby actor probing the vulnerable parser (CFG is disabled in the app, making the UAF potentially exploitable). Rationale: Used the exact Windows client binary (nearby_share.exe, C:\Program Files\Google\Nearby Share) tied to the article's V6 heap use-after-free in Google Quick Share for Windows; WerFault parent-of-crashed-process (Defender/Sysmon/FDR) and Application Error EID 1000 (Sentinel) are the only host-side artifacts the crash leaves. Binary name and the six-flaw breakdown (V6 = Windows UAF) cross-checked against the CISPA arxiv preprint and Help Net Security. Cross-checked against: • https://arxiv.org/html/2606.26967v1 • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/30/apple-airdrop-google-samsung-quick-share-vulnerabilities/ • https://www.spyshelter.com/exe/google-llc-quicksharesetup-exe/
ATT&CKT1499.004 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Quick Share instability crashing nearby_share.exe during a large or interrupted file transfer
  • A crash immediately following a Google/Quick Share auto-update where a stale component is loaded
  • GPU/display-driver fault tearing down the app's window and tripping WER
  • Corrupt user profile or .NET/runtime issue causing the same app to crash repeatedly for one user
  • Internal QA/red-team reproducing the published CISPA PoC tooling against test hosts
Suppression filter
| extend BurstMinutes = datetime_diff('minute', LastCrash, FirstCrash)
| where CrashCount >= 3 and BurstMinutes <= 15   // rapid repeated crashes (looped probing) rather than a one-off app bug or post-update crash
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the crashing image is C:\Program Files\Google\Nearby Share\nearby_share.exe and check the burst timing — multiple crashes within minutes on a host whose Quick Share is set to 'Everyone' visibility is the high-fidelity case. Check the installed Quick Share version vs Google's latest fixed build. 2) CONTAIN: Set Quick Share visibility off / out of 'Everyone', or stop nearby_share.exe, on affected hosts; if the host is in a high-density area (airport/conference/office floor) treat as active proximity probing and isolate Wi-Fi/Bluetooth if exploitation is suspected. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the same host's DeviceNetworkEvents for inbound local-subnet connections to nearby_share.exe just before each crash, look for the same crash pattern on other hosts in the same physical location/subnet (indicates one attacker hitting many devices), and confirm all endpoints are on the patched Quick Share build.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "WerFault.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "nearby_share.exe" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Google\Nearby Share"
| summarize CrashCount = count(), FirstCrash = min(Timestamp), LastCrash = max(Timestamp), SampleCmd = any(ProcessCommandLine)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| where CrashCount >= 2   // 1 crash = benign app bug; >=2 crashes of a network-facing sharing service => likely V6 UAF probing
| order by CrashCount desc
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventLog == "Application"
| where Source == "Application Error"   // Windows Error Reporting app-crash record
| where EventID == 1000
| where RenderedDescription has "nearby_share.exe"
| summarize CrashCount = count(), FirstCrash = min(TimeGenerated), LastCrash = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer
| where CrashCount >= 2   // repeated crashes of the Quick Share client => likely active V6 UAF probing rather than a one-off
| order by CrashCount desc
