Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks

    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:

level: high

Internet-facing Oracle PeopleSoft exposed/exploited via CVE-2026-35273 PSEMHUB SSRF (ShinyHunters) AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces internet-facing PeopleSoft hosts carrying CVE-2026-35273 and anomalous access to the Environment Management Hub (PSEMHUB) servlet — the unauthenticated SSRF→RCE entry point ShinyHunters/UNC6240 exploited as a zero-day between May 27 and June 9 2026. Pairs vulnerability exposure with the specific exploited endpoint so SOC can prioritise the actual attack surface, not a generic CVE list. Rationale: Anchored on the corroborated exploited component (PSEMHUB / Environment Management Hub) and the exact CVE id CVE-2026-35273 (CVSS 9.8 unauth SSRF→RCE), not a generic web-exploit template. PSEMHUB is an internal hub rarely reached externally, so external hits are high-fidelity. Defender path is vuln-exposure, Sentinel path is the exploit endpoint. Cross-checked against: • https://www.oracle.com/security-alerts/alert-cve-2026-35273.html • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-active-exploitation-of-oracle-peoplesoft-zero-day-cve-2026-35273/ • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/shinyhunters-targets-education-sector-oracle-exploit
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate PeopleSoft Environment Management Hub agents (PSEMAgent) checking in to PSEMHUB from internal app/batch servers
  • Internal Oracle/PeopleSoft admins browsing PSEMHUB during environment configuration
  • Vulnerability scanners (Qualys/Tenable/Rapid7) probing PSEMHUB and PSIGW paths
  • Load-balancer or uptime health checks hitting the PeopleSoft web tier
  • PeopleSoft Integration Broker (PSIGW) normal SOAP traffic from trusted partners
Suppression filter
| where cIP !startswith "10." and cIP !startswith "192.168." and cIP !startswith "172.16."
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the hitting cIP is external/untrusted and whether the PeopleTools version (8.61/8.62/8.63) is unpatched for CVE-2026-35273; review PSEMHUB request bodies/user-agents for SSRF markers. 2) Contain: apply Oracle's emergency mitigation/patch, restrict PSEMHUB and PSIGW to internal/management networks via WAF/ACL, and snapshot the host for forensics. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2/UC3 on the same host — look for java-spawned shells, MeshCentral/node.exe, and outbound to azurenetfiles.net or 142.11.200.184/29.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-35273"
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(1d)
    | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP) by DeviceId
  ) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by IsInternetFacing desc
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem has "/PSEMHUB" or csUriStem has "/PSIGW"
| summarize Requests=count(), Methods=make_set(csMethod), Statuses=make_set(scStatus), TotalRespBytes=sum(scBytes), Clients=make_set(cIP, 50) by Computer, csUriStem, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="*/PSEMHUB*" OR Web.url="*/PSIGW*" by Web.src Web.dest Web.http_method Web.url Web.status Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where status!=404 AND status!=403 | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="*/PSEMHUB*" OR Web.url="*/PSIGW*" by Web.src Web.dest Web.http_method Web.url Web.status Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where status!=404 AND status!=403 | sort - lastTime
Oracle PeopleSoft Java/app-server process spawning shell or recon binary (CVE-2026-35273 post-exploit) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the PeopleSoft web/app tier (WebLogic java.exe, psae.exe, PSEMAgent.exe, psadmin.exe) spawning command shells, LOLBins, node.exe, or AD-recon utilities — the hands-on-keyboard activity Mandiant observed after CVE-2026-35273 RCE (internal PeopleSoft recon, lateral-movement scripts, MeshCentral install). A PeopleSoft Java process spawning cmd/powershell is abnormal and indicates code execution through the exploited servlet. Rationale: Article-specific because the parent set is the PeopleSoft web/app tier and the child set mirrors Mandiant's reported post-exploit behaviour (internal PeopleSoft recon, lateral-movement scripting, node.exe for MeshCentral). A Java/PeopleTools process spawning a shell is the textbook signal of the CVE-2026-35273 RCE being used. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/shinyhunters-targets-education-sector-oracle-exploit • https://www.securityweek.com/google-confirms-exploitation-of-oracle-peoplesoft-zero-day-by-shinyhunters/
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • PeopleSoft Process Scheduler / App Engine (psae.exe) legitimately invoking cmd.exe wrappers for batch jobs
  • Admin/DevOps shell scripts launched from a Java-based management console
  • PeopleTools COBOL/SQR batch processing that shells out to net.exe for share access
  • Monitoring agents querying whoami/net during inventory collection
  • Application deployment automation running certutil for cert installs
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "cmd.exe" and InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "psae.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("PS_HOME","PRCSRQST","psprcs"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child ProcessCommandLine for recon (whoami/nltest/net group), download (certutil/bitsadmin/curl), or MeshCentral (node.exe) strings, and confirm the host is a PeopleSoft server. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the offending process tree, and capture parent java.exe command line + loaded modules. 3) Hunt: check UC3 for outbound to azurenetfiles.net / 142.11.200.184/29, UC5 for the listed file hashes, and UC4 for .zst staging archives on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("java.exe","psae.exe","PSEMAgent.exe","psadmin.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\PeopleSoft\", @"\pt8.6", @"\PT8.6")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","node.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","nltest.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("java.exe","psae.exe","PSEMAgent.exe","psadmin.exe")

PeopleSoft host beaconing to ShinyHunters MeshCentral C2 (azurenetfiles.net / 142.11.200.184-29 / 176.120.22.24) AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on DNS resolution of azurenetfiles.net and outbound sessions from internal hosts to ShinyHunters infrastructure: the MeshCentral C2 wss://azurenetfiles.net:443/agent.ashx, the staging IPs 142.11.200.186-190 (Python SimpleHTTP on 8888) and 176.120.22.24. Server segments should virtually never initiate this egress, making it high-fidelity for the CVE-2026-35273 data-theft campaign. Rationale: Every indicator is externally corroborated: azurenetfiles.net is the hardcoded MeshCentral C2 (wss://azurenetfiles.net:443/agent.ashx), 142.11.200.186-190 hosted attacker Python SimpleHTTP staging on port 8888, and the IPs shared a TLS cert CN of azurenetfiles.net. Server-tier egress to these is near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/oracle-peoplesoft-servers-hacked-in-shinyhunters-data-theft-attacks/ • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/shinyhunters-targets-education-sector-oracle-exploit • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4184408/oracle-peoplesoft-zero%E2%80%91day-fuels-shinyhunters-extortion-spree.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1219 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/EDR sandbox detonation or sinkhole infrastructure resolving azurenetfiles.net for research
  • Security team validating IOCs by intentionally connecting to the listed IPs
  • Proxy/secure-web-gateway logging the blocked connection (already-mitigated TP, not benign)
  • IP reuse: 176.120.22.24 or the 142.11.200.0/24 block reassigned to a benign tenant after takedown
  • Internal DNS resolver forwarding a downstream client's query (attribute to true source IP)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "Windows Defender")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process/host — if it is a PeopleSoft server or the InitiatingProcess is node.exe/java.exe, treat as confirmed C2; check for the MeshCentral agent.ashx URL. 2) Contain: block azurenetfiles.net and 142.11.200.184/29 + 176.120.22.24 at firewall/proxy/DNS, isolate the host, and terminate the MeshCentral/node process and its service. 3) Hunt: review UC4 for zstd staging archives, UC2 for the spawning java process, and pull all sessions to 142.11.200.184/29:8888 to scope exfiltrated data volume.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "azurenetfiles.net"
    or ipv4_is_in_range(RemoteIP, "142.11.200.184/29")
    or RemoteIP == "176.120.22.24"
| extend MeshCentralC2 = (RemoteUrl has "agent.ashx" and RemoteUrl has "azurenetfiles.net")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, MeshCentralC2, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(
    ImDnsActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DnsQuery has "azurenetfiles.net"
    | project TimeGenerated, Src=SrcIpAddr, Host=SrcHostname, Indicator=DnsQuery, Channel="DNS"
),
(
    CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DestinationIP == "176.120.22.24" or ipv4_is_in_range(DestinationIP, "142.11.200.184/29") or DestinationDnsDomain has "azurenetfiles.net"
    | project TimeGenerated, Src=SourceIP, Host=SourceHostName, Indicator=strcat(DestinationIP, ":", tostring(DestinationPort)), Channel="Firewall"
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

zstd data-staging archives written on PeopleSoft host (ShinyHunters exfil prep) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects creation of zstd-compressed archives (.zst / .tar.zst) on server-tier hosts by PeopleSoft, node.exe (MeshCentral), shell or scripting processes — the compression method Mandiant observed ShinyHunters using to stage HR/payroll data for exfiltration after CVE-2026-35273. zstd archiving on a PeopleSoft application server is abnormal and immediately precedes egress to attacker staging servers. Rationale: zstd compression is the corroborated, distinctive staging TTP Mandiant tied to this campaign, and scoping the writer process to the PeopleSoft/MeshCentral tier separates it from generic compression. Sorting by file size surfaces the bulk HR/payroll archives. Cross-checked against: • https://www.securityweek.com/google-confirms-exploitation-of-oracle-peoplesoft-zero-day-by-shinyhunters/ • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/shinyhunters-targets-education-sector-oracle-exploit
ATT&CKT1560.001 T1567 T1213
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate backup tooling that uses zstd compression (e.g. Borg, restic, PostgreSQL/MongoDB dumps with zstd)
  • Developers compressing logs or build artifacts with zstd on a server
  • Container image layer extraction writing .zst blobs
  • PeopleSoft log-rotation or data-export jobs that legitimately produce compressed archives
  • Filesystem replication/sync tools transferring pre-compressed .zst files
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Veeam\", @"\restic", @"\borg", @"\Commvault\") or FolderPath has_any (@"\Backup\", @"\backups\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the .zst path, size, and parent command line — large archives in temp/web dirs written by node.exe/java.exe/psae.exe are suspect; confirm host is a PeopleSoft data store. 2) Contain: isolate the host, preserve the archive for scoping which PII tables were collected, and block egress to UC3 destinations. 3) Hunt: correlate the file-write time to outbound sessions to 142.11.200.184/29:8888 (staging) and azurenetfiles.net, and check other PeopleSoft hosts for the same .zst pattern.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName endswith ".zst" or FileName endswith ".tar.zst"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("zstd.exe","zstd","node.exe","java.exe","psae.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","bash","sh","python.exe","python3")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, FileSize, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by FileSize desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName endswith ".zst"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("zstd","node.exe","java.exe","psae.exe","powershell","pwsh","cmd.exe","bash","sh","python")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSize, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TargetFileSize desc

Known ShinyHunters PeopleSoft payload/staging file hashes on disk (CVE-2026-35273) AIInstallation Medium
Alerts on any of the five SHA256 hashes tied to the CVE-2026-35273 PeopleSoft intrusions appearing in file-write or process-execution telemetry. Pure IOC match for the campaign's dropped web shells/staging tooling, giving an immediate high-confidence hit on affected hosts. Rationale: Direct SHA256 IOC match against the five campaign hashes from the article's IOC set; hash hits are unambiguous and warrant alerting tier. Union of file-write and process-exec catches both the drop and any subsequent execution. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/nissan-discloses-employee-data-breach-linked-to-oracle-zero-day-attacks/ • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-active-exploitation-of-oracle-peoplesoft-zero-day-cve-2026-35273/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hash collision is cryptographically negligible — near-zero benign FP
  • Security team intentionally placing the IOC sample on a sandbox/analysis host
  • EDR quarantine copies of the file re-triggering the file-write detection
  • Backup/AV scan re-reading the quarantined sample
  • Threat-intel platform caching the sample for enrichment
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any (@"\Quarantine", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\VirusShare", @"\Malware\Samples\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the hash hit and capture the file path/host; if on a PeopleSoft server, treat as confirmed compromise. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the file, terminate any running instance, and preserve memory/disk for forensics. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for all five hashes, then pivot to UC2 (java→shell), UC3 (azurenetfiles.net / staging-IP C2), and UC4 (.zst archives) on every host that matched.

union
(DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where SHA256 in (badHashes) | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Source="FileWrite", FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, Actor=InitiatingProcessFileName, Cmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
(DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where SHA256 in (badHashes) | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Source="ProcessExec", FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, Actor=InitiatingProcessFileName, Cmd=ProcessCommandLine)
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileSHA256 in ("f02a924c9ff92a8780ce812511341182c6b509d45bc59f3f7b522e37225d24fc","d83fdb9e53c5ff03c4cb0451ea1bebd79b53f29eadc1e2fa394c7af13a86ce2f","c7e9332731b06644fc73e0046a2a89eaa59b09f54250e9bd622467187351711f","68257a6f9ff196179ec03624e849927f26599eb180a7c82e14ef5bc4e93bc309","2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("f02a924c9ff92a8780ce812511341182c6b509d45bc59f3f7b522e37225d24fc", "d83fdb9e53c5ff03c4cb0451ea1bebd79b53f29eadc1e2fa394c7af13a86ce2f", "c7e9332731b06644fc73e0046a2a89eaa59b09f54250e9bd622467187351711f", "68257a6f9ff196179ec03624e849927f26599eb180a7c82e14ef5bc4e93bc309", "2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35") or SHA1 in~ ("f02a924c9ff92a8780ce812511341182c6b509d45bc59f3f7b522e37225d24fc", "d83fdb9e53c5ff03c4cb0451ea1bebd79b53f29eadc1e2fa394c7af13a86ce2f", "c7e9332731b06644fc73e0046a2a89eaa59b09f54250e9bd622467187351711f", "68257a6f9ff196179ec03624e849927f26599eb180a7c82e14ef5bc4e93bc309", "2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35") or MD5 in~ ("f02a924c9ff92a8780ce812511341182c6b509d45bc59f3f7b522e37225d24fc", "d83fdb9e53c5ff03c4cb0451ea1bebd79b53f29eadc1e2fa394c7af13a86ce2f", "c7e9332731b06644fc73e0046a2a89eaa59b09f54250e9bd622467187351711f", "68257a6f9ff196179ec03624e849927f26599eb180a7c82e14ef5bc4e93bc309", "2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("f02a924c9ff92a8780ce812511341182c6b509d45bc59f3f7b522e37225d24fc", "d83fdb9e53c5ff03c4cb0451ea1bebd79b53f29eadc1e2fa394c7af13a86ce2f", "c7e9332731b06644fc73e0046a2a89eaa59b09f54250e9bd622467187351711f", "68257a6f9ff196179ec03624e849927f26599eb180a7c82e14ef5bc4e93bc309", "2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35") or SHA1 in~ ("f02a924c9ff92a8780ce812511341182c6b509d45bc59f3f7b522e37225d24fc", "d83fdb9e53c5ff03c4cb0451ea1bebd79b53f29eadc1e2fa394c7af13a86ce2f", "c7e9332731b06644fc73e0046a2a89eaa59b09f54250e9bd622467187351711f", "68257a6f9ff196179ec03624e849927f26599eb180a7c82e14ef5bc4e93bc309", "2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35") or MD5 in~ ("f02a924c9ff92a8780ce812511341182c6b509d45bc59f3f7b522e37225d24fc", "d83fdb9e53c5ff03c4cb0451ea1bebd79b53f29eadc1e2fa394c7af13a86ce2f", "c7e9332731b06644fc73e0046a2a89eaa59b09f54250e9bd622467187351711f", "68257a6f9ff196179ec03624e849927f26599eb180a7c82e14ef5bc4e93bc309", "2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["f02a924c9ff92a8780ce812511341182c6b509d45bc59f3f7b522e37225d24fc", "d83fdb9e53c5ff03c4cb0451ea1bebd79b53f29eadc1e2fa394c7af13a86ce2f", "c7e9332731b06644fc73e0046a2a89eaa59b09f54250e9bd622467187351711f", "68257a6f9ff196179ec03624e849927f26599eb180a7c82e14ef5bc4e93bc309", "2ab684d93c1553fad87041b4dea97188a97e78589deee2a7bacff905564f3a35"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious Perplexity Chrome Extension Intercepted Searches and Address Bar Input

The Hacker News
2026-06-29 9 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Microsoft has found a malicious Chrome extension that posed as the AI search engine Perplexity and quietly logged what people searched for. It routed every query and every character typed into the address bar through an attacker-controlled server before redirecting users to real results. Microsoft says Google removed it from the store after responsible disclosure. The extension was called "

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Malicious 'Search for perplexity ai' Chrome/Edge extension install by ID flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd · Suspicious browser extension installation · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Browser search/suggest traffic to Perplexity look-alike C2 domain perplexity-ai.online · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Malicious 'Search for perplexity ai' Chrome/Edge extension install by ID flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd AIInstallation High
Hunts on-disk installation of the specific malicious Chromium extension Microsoft flagged as posing as Perplexity AI, identified by its globally-unique Web Store ID flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd written under the browser Extensions profile directory. Because the extension ID is a hard, unique IOC, any host with this folder is compromised regardless of how the bytes arrived. Rationale: Pivots on the single hardest IOC in the article — the Chrome Web Store extension ID flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd, which appears verbatim as the on-disk Extensions sub-folder name; it is globally unique so presence equals compromise. Corroborated by Microsoft's own Security Blog (detected as PUA:Win32/SearchHijacker). Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/29/chromium-extension-uses-airelated-branding-redirect-browser-search/ • https://windowsnews.ai/article/microsoft-flags-malicious-perplexity-ai-extension-stealing-search-traffic-on-windows.432081
ATT&CKT1176 T1204.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware-analysis / sandbox host intentionally installing the extension for research detonation
  • Forensic or backup tooling copying a Chrome/Edge profile that still contains the quarantined extension folder
  • Threat-intel sync or SOAR job writing IOC artifact files that embed the extension-ID string
  • Defender/EDR quarantine or removal process re-touching the extension directory during cleanup
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the FolderPath is under a real browser profile (…\User Data\Default\Extensions\) and that the writing process is chrome.exe/msedge.exe rather than a backup/AV tool; identify the user and install time. 2) Contain: instruct the user to remove the extension, force a managed-browser policy to block extension ID flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd, and reset the default search engine; isolate only if other malicious activity is present. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2 — query the same DeviceId for outbound traffic to perplexity-ai.online to confirm searches were exfiltrated, and sweep the fleet for the same extension ID on other hosts.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd" or FileName has "flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Browser search/suggest traffic to Perplexity look-alike C2 domain perplexity-ai.online AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts outbound browser connections (and DNS resolutions) to the attacker-controlled look-alike domain perplexity-ai[.]online, where the malicious extension routed every search query and every character typed into the address bar (suggest_url) before redirecting to a real engine. Distinct from the legitimate perplexity.ai, so a single match indicates active search/keystroke exfiltration. Rationale: Matches the article's only network IOC — the look-alike C2 domain perplexity-ai[.]online — using has/contains so the legitimate perplexity.ai is not matched, and scopes the Defender variant to browser processes to confirm it is the extension's redirect/suggest_url channel. Domain confirmed by Microsoft Security Blog and secondary press coverage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/29/chromium-extension-uses-airelated-branding-redirect-browser-search/ • https://windowsnews.ai/article/microsoft-flags-malicious-perplexity-ai-extension-stealing-search-traffic-on-windows.432081
ATT&CKT1185 T1041 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or sandbox detonating the extension/domain for analysis
  • URL-reputation or detonation engines (Defender SmartScreen, urlscan, VirusTotal nodes) resolving the domain to categorize it
  • Threat-intel feed validation jobs actively probing the IOC
  • Corporate web proxy pre-fetch or DNS sinkhole answering for the blocked domain (sinkhole IP in answer)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","SenseIR.exe","MsSense.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the resolving/initiating process is a browser and not a scanner/sinkhole; capture the user, host, and whether the DNS answer is a real attacker IP vs a sinkhole. 2) Contain: block perplexity-ai.online at DNS/proxy/firewall, push a managed-browser policy resetting the default search provider, and remove the extension (pivot to UC1 for the on-disk artifact). 3) Hunt: review the user's recent search/address-bar activity for sensitive data that may have been logged, sweep DNS logs fleet-wide for the same domain to scope the install footprint, and check for the disabled-but-present Google/Bing redirect rules being switched on.

| where RemoteUrl has "perplexity-ai.online"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","chrome_proxy.exe")

| order by Timestamp desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Critical

Chromium extension uses AI‑related branding to redirect browser search

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-06-29 10 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A malicious Chromium-based extension that spoofs the AI-powered answer engine Perplexity AI redirects browser search traffic using MV3 APIs and intermediary infrastructure. The post Chromium extension uses AI‑related branding to redirect browser search appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

ATT&CKT1176 T1190 T1566
Domainsperplexity-ai.online oda.digital extension.tilda.ws

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Chromium extension uses AI‑related branding to redirect browser search
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Malicious Perplexity-spoofing extension ID flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd written to disk · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Search-interception traffic to Perplexity typosquat domain perplexity-ai[.]online · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Search-interception traffic to Perplexity typosquat domain perplexity-ai[.]online AICommand & Control High
Hunts browser connections/DNS resolutions to the attacker-controlled search-interception infrastructure (perplexity-ai.online and related oda.digital / extension.tilda.ws) used by the fake 'Search for perplexity ai' Chromium extension. Because the extension routes every Omnibox query and keystroke-level suggestion through this domain before redirecting to a real engine, any browser-originated traffic to these hosts is high-fidelity evidence of an infected endpoint. Rationale: Anchored on the exact interception domain perplexity-ai.online (confirmed by both the MSFT blog and The Hacker News) plus the pre-extracted secondary infra oda.digital / extension.tilda.ws, scoped to browser parent processes — a typosquat domain reached by a browser is near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/malicious-perplexity-chrome-extension.html • https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/search-for-perplexity-ai/flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd • https://www.crx4chrome.com/extensions/flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1176 T1185
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC/IR analyst detonating the extension sample in a managed sandbox host
  • Web proxy / secure-web-gateway pre-fetching or URL-categorizing the domain on a user's behalf
  • Threat-intel enrichment or DNS-sinkhole tooling resolving the IOC for blocking
  • A user who clicked the lookalike landing page once but did not install (single browse vs. repeated query routing)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which device/user generated the traffic and whether the 'Search for perplexity ai' extension (ID flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd) is installed; check if default search provider was overridden to perplexity-ai.online. 2) Contain: force-remove the extension via browser policy/ExtensionInstallBlocklist, reset the default search engine, and block perplexity-ai.online / oda.digital / extension.tilda.ws at proxy and DNS. 3) Hunt: pivot on all other hosts resolving these domains and review browsing/search history routed through the domain for sensitive query exposure during the exposure window.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("perplexity-ai.online","oda.digital","extension.tilda.ws")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","vivaldi.exe","chrome_proxy.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any ("perplexity-ai.online","oda.digital","extension.tilda.ws")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode, ResultCodeName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: DNS Query to Perplexity Typosquat Search-Interception Domain
id: 5b3e9a42-7c1f-4d2a-9f6e-2a1c8d4b7e90
description: Detects DNS resolution of perplexity-ai.online and related infrastructure used by a malicious Chromium extension spoofing Perplexity AI to intercept browser search queries.
references:
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/29/chromium-extension-uses-airelated-branding-redirect-browser-search/
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/malicious-perplexity-chrome-extension.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/29
tags:
  - attack.t1071.001
  - attack.t1176
  - attack.command_and_control
logsource:
  category: dns
detection:
  selection:
    QueryName|contains:
      - perplexity-ai.online
      - oda.digital
      - extension.tilda.ws
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationHostname:(*perplexity-ai.online* OR *oda.digital* OR extension.tilda.ws)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(perplexity-ai\.online|oda\.digital|extension\.tilda\.ws)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where (DNS.query="*perplexity-ai.online*" OR DNS.query="*oda.digital*" OR DNS.query="extension.tilda.ws") by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where (DNS.query="*perplexity-ai.online*" OR DNS.query="*oda.digital*" OR DNS.query="extension.tilda.ws") by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Malicious Perplexity-spoofing extension ID flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd written to disk AIInstallation High
Hunts for the unique Chrome Web Store extension ID flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd ('Search for perplexity ai') appearing in browser extension folder paths or written files on managed endpoints. The extension ID is a globally unique 32-char identifier, so any file-system artifact bearing it is a deterministic indicator that the taken-down malicious search hijacker was installed. Rationale: The 32-char extension ID flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd is a globally unique store identifier (confirmed via the Chrome Web Store and crx4chrome listings), so its presence in any extension folder path is a deterministic install indicator with effectively no collisions. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/malicious-perplexity-chrome-extension.html • https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/search-for-perplexity-ai/flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd • https://www.crx4chrome.com/extensions/flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd/
ATT&CKT1176 T1185
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint backup software capturing the Chrome 'User Data' profile directory that still contains the extension folder
  • IR/forensic collection tooling copying browser profiles for offline analysis
  • AV/EDR scanning or quarantining the extension folder (file-access touches the path)
  • Sync of an already-infected profile to a new device via Chrome profile sync before takedown
Suppression filter
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the ActionType (FileCreated = fresh install vs FileDeleted = remediation) and identify the user profile and browser hosting the extension folder. 2) Contain: remove the extension, push it to the browser ExtensionInstallBlocklist policy, and reset the hijacked default search provider; block perplexity-ai.online at DNS/proxy. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1 network telemetry to confirm queries were exfiltrated, and sweep the fleet for the same extension ID to find all installs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, FileOriginUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "flkebkiofojicogddingbdmcmkpbplcd"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, DvcAction, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic([""]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["perplexity-ai.online", "oda.digital", "extension.tilda.ws"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.

            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

UNC5792/UNC4221 Signal & WhatsApp typosquat lure-domain resolution AIDelivery High
Hunts endpoint DNS/network resolutions to the specific Signal/WhatsApp lookalike domains used by Russian-linked UNC5792/UNC4221 to host fake group-invite and 2FA pages. Article-specific because it pins the exact actor-controlled typosquat domain list rather than a generic 'phishing domain' heuristic. Rationale: Uses the exact UNC5792/UNC4221 typosquat domain list (signal-group*, *-signal*, signal-security*, signal-device-off*) cross-checked against the FBI/CISA IC3 PSA I-062626 and Google/Mandiant 'Signals of Trouble' report; named IOC domains make this high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2026/PSA260626 • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/russia-targeting-signal-messenger/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fbi-russian-hackers-now-target-signal-backup-recovery-keys/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1656
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel analyst manually browsing the IOC domains in an isolated VM/sandbox
  • EDR/SOAR automated URL detonation resolving the domains during enrichment
  • Security proxy or DNS sinkhole resolving the domains to a block page
  • A targeted user who clicked the lure to 'investigate' and self-reported
  • Threat-feed enrichment service pre-resolving submitted IOCs
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe","SenseSampleUploader.exe","MsMpEng.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the device/user that resolved the domain and the initiating process (browser vs. tooling); confirm it is a real user and not a sandbox/proxy host. 2) Contain: block all 20 typosquat domains at proxy/DNS, force-reset the user's Signal/messaging session, and instruct the user to open Signal > Linked Devices and remove unknown devices and rotate the backup recovery key. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same device/user for the sgnl://linkdevice URI (UC3) and inbound mail/DMs from fake 'Signal support' accounts; sweep the org for any other host resolving these domains.

Inbound mail delivering UNC5792 Signal recovery-key lure domains AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound email whose embedded URLs point to the UNC5792/UNC4221 Signal/WhatsApp typosquat domains. Although the campaign primarily uses in-app DMs, the same actor domains are also distributed via email; this surfaces delivery to mailboxes of high-value targets. Rationale: Joins EmailEvents to EmailUrlInfo on the exact actor typosquat domains so only mail carrying a UNC5792 lure URL fires; sender impersonation of 'Signal support' plus a typosquat link is high-fidelity. Sentinel/Datadog/Falcon/Splunk left empty because EmailUrlInfo has no equivalent in those telemetry sets (mail-flow URL data lives only in Defender XDR for this tenant). Cross-checked against: • https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2026/PSA260626 • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/russia-targeting-signal-messenger/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1598
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal phishing-simulation platform using look-alike domains for training
  • A user forwarding a reported phishing email internally (inbound to the SOC mailbox)
  • Threat-intel newsletter or vendor advisory email quoting the IOC domains as text/links
  • Security awareness team distributing screenshots of the lure with the domain visible
Suppression filter
| where SenderFromDomain !endswith "yourphishingsim-vendor.com" and DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the message is external/inbound and the URL host is one of the actor domains (not a quoted IOC in an advisory); check DeliveryAction/DeliveryLocation to see if it reached the inbox. 2) Contain: soft-delete/quarantine the message tenant-wide via the NetworkMessageId, block the sender and domains, and check UrlClickEvents for whether the recipient clicked. 3) Hunt: if clicked, pivot the recipient to UC1 (domain resolution) and UC3 (device-link URI), and review the user's Signal linked devices and recovery-key status.

Signal linked-device hijack URI (sgnl://linkdevice) & recovery-key lure pages AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the UNC5792 device-linking abuse signature — the sgnl://linkdevice?uuid= deep-link Mandiant documented in fake Signal group-invite pages — plus web-proxy hits to the recovery-key/2FA harvest domains. This is the actual account-takeover mechanism, distinct from generic domain resolution. Rationale: Pivots on the Mandiant-documented sgnl://linkdevice?uuid= device-linking URI (the persistent-eavesdrop mechanism) and the credential-harvest domain subset (signal-security*, signal-device-off*, *-confirm*) tied to the recovery-key/2FA ruse; both cross-checked against Google/Mandiant and IC3 PSA. Confidence Medium because deep-link capture depends on full-URL proxy/command-line telemetry being present. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/russia-targeting-signal-messenger/ • https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2026/PSA260626
ATT&CKT1621 T1111 T1656
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate user genuinely linking a second Signal desktop/iPad via an official sgnl://linkdevice link
  • QA/IT testing of Signal desktop provisioning on managed devices
  • Security researcher reproducing the Mandiant device-link PoC in a lab
  • Proxy logging an official signal.org-hosted link rendered with the same scheme
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has "sgnl://linkdevice" and (RemoteUrl has "signal.org" or RemoteUrl has "//signal.me/"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether the sgnl://linkdevice URI / lure-domain hit originated from an official Signal flow (signal.org) or from one of the actor typosquat domains; identify the user and host. 2) Contain: instruct the user to open Signal > Linked Devices, remove any unrecognized linked device immediately, rotate the backup recovery key, and re-register; block the credential-harvest domains. 3) Hunt: review the prior 7 days for the same user receiving 'Signal support' impersonation contact, resolutions to other typosquat domains (UC1), and any inbound mail lures (UC2); check for unusual message-history access on the account.
let CredLures = dynamic(["signal-security.online","signal-security.site","signal-device-off.online","signal-confirm.site","confirm-signal.site","signal-protect.host"]);
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (RemoteUrl has "sgnl://linkdevice" or ProcessCommandLine has "sgnl://linkdevice" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "sgnl://linkdevice")
    or RemoteUrl has_any (CredLures)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ActionType, RemoteUrl, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,

| order by TimeGenerated desc
